title: SHE WAS SUMMONED.
paragraphs: SHE WAS SUMMONED.

Not seduced.
Not scheming.
Not prowling on a rooftop.
Summoned.
And that one word changes the room.

Open your Bible to 2 Samuel 11. It doesn’t say she sent for the king. It says the king sent for her.
Power moved first. Authority initiated. The crown knocked on her door.
And when a king summons you in ancient Israel, you don’t ignore it. You go.
Let’s slow this down.

Night air. Rooftop breeze. Bathwater still clinging to skin. Droplets tracing down her arms, catching the last crimson streaks of sunset. She is cleansing, not performing. Obeying the Law’s purification rites (2 Samuel 11:4).

Then footsteps.
Armor.
A command.
“The king has sent for you.”
Fear doesn’t announce itself loudly. Sometimes it whispers.
She went.
And history blamed her.
But the text does not.

The text says David sent.
The text says David inquired.
The text says David took.
That verb. Took.
This is not a romance. This is power without restraint. Desire without discipline. An anointed king acting like a predator.

And here is the open wound:
The man after God’s own heart used his position to feed his appetite.
Let that sit.

Because some of you know what it feels like to be summoned by someone with power.
Boss.
Leader.
Pastor.
Influencer.
Family friend.
Summoned.
And afterward, silence swallowed your side of the story.

But Scripture does not erase her. It names her. Over and over. “The wife of Uriah.”
She had covenant. She had dignity. She had a life before this chapter.
Then pregnancy.
Then panic.
Then a corpse on a battlefield because the king tried to bury his sin in blood.
This is what unchecked desire does. It consumes innocence and calls it collateral damage.
And the Bible says something chilling:
“But the thing that David had done displeased the Lord.” (2 Samuel 11:27)

Heaven saw.
Heaven recorded.
Heaven was not confused about who moved first.
Now here’s where grace storms in.
Because the story does not end in chapter 11.

Enter Nathan.
Enter confrontation.
Enter repentance.
Psalm 51 bleeds out of David’s brokenness.
And Bathsheba?
She becomes the mother of Solomon.
Not the child conceived in violence — that child dies under the weight of David’s sin. But later, after repentance, after mercy, God gives another son.
Solomon.
And trace the genealogy forward.
Through Solomon’s line comes Jesus Christ.
Do you see it?

God does not endorse the abuse.
God does not excuse the sin.
God judges it.
But God also redeems what shame tried to erase.
Bathsheba is not remembered as “the temptress.”

In Matthew 1, she is folded into the lineage of Christ.
The Messiah carries her story in His bloodline.
That is not accidental.

That is God saying:
“I will not let power define you. I will not let someone else’s sin have the final word.”

Maybe you were summoned into something you didn’t choose.
Maybe someone else’s authority left scars on your story.
Maybe the world whispered that it was your fault.
Hear me clearly:
Jesus does not echo that lie.

He confronts abusers.
He defends the vulnerable.
He restores the shamed.
He carries wounded women — and broken men — into redemption.

David needed repentance.
Bathsheba needed dignity restored.
And we need a Savior who deals with both sin and suffering.
That Savior is Christ.

The cross is where abusive power dies.
The resurrection is where stolen stories are rewritten.

So if you’re carrying shame that isn’t yours — bring it to Him.
If you’re carrying sin that is yours — bring that too.

There is mercy for the repentant.
There is healing for the wounded.

And there is a King greater than David
who never summons to exploit —
only calls to save.
